core.text: To say *longer, heavier, more beautiful*, Latin puts *-ior* on the adjective's stem: **the comparative (the '-er / more' form)**. *longus* (long) → *longior*; *gravis* (heavy) → *gravior*; *pulcher* (beautiful) → *pulchrior*. The neuter is *-ius*: *pīlum brevius* — a shorter spear. The other endings are the 3rd-declension ones: *longiōrem, longiōris, longiōrēs, longiōra*. The thing you compare with follows *quam* (than), in the same case as the first thing: *gladius longior est quam pīlum*. Latin name: gradus comparātīvus.
The comparative is the *-er* or *more* form: *taller, more careful*. *Than* introduces the point of comparison: *taller than his brother*.
Stem + -ior (neuter -ius), declined like a 3rd-declension noun; 'than' = quam, same case on both sides.

invented.en: The road is longer than the stream.

core.text: *-ior* means *more* (two things side by side); *-issimus* means *most* (one against all the rest). *Februārius brevior est quam Mārtius* sets two months against each other; *mēnsis brevissimus* picks the shortest of all twelve. The endings differ too: the comparative declines like a 3rd-declension noun (*breviōrem*), the superlative (the '-est / most' form) like *bonus -a -um* (*brevissimum*).

teach.title: What it does
teach.say: Put two things side by side and Latin marks the adjective: **the comparative (the '-er / more' form)**. *longus* (long) → *longior* (longer); *fortis* (brave) → *fortior* (braver). It says one of the two has more of the quality than the other — no more than that.

check.ask: Which word is the comparative, and who is Quintus being set against?

teach.title: How it is built: stem + -ior
teach.say: One cell. Take the adjective's stem — the part left when you strip the dictionary ending — and add *-ior*: *long-* → *longior*, *fort-* → *fortior*, *laet-* → *laetior*, *alt-* → *altior*. That is the masculine and feminine subject form; masculine and feminine are alike in this family.

show.say: longior — the stem long- with -ior on it, for a masculine or a feminine noun

check.ask: Give the comparative subject form of *longus* — the one masculine and feminine share.

teach.title: The neuter is -ius
teach.say: One cell more. With a neuter noun the ending is *-ius*, not *-ior*: *scūtum brevius* (a shorter shield), *crūs longius* (a longer leg). Same stem, different last syllable.

show.say: longius — same stem, -ius instead of -ior, for a neuter noun

teach.title: The rest of the endings are 3rd-declension ones
teach.say: Beyond those two cells the comparative declines like a 3rd-declension noun on the stem *-iōr-*: the accusative (the object form) *-iōrem* (*longiōrem*), the genitive (the 'of' form) *-iōris*, the plural nominative *-iōrēs* and the neuter plural *-iōra* (*graviōra*). Nothing new to learn — endings you already know, on a new stem.

show.say: longiōrem / longiōrēs — 3rd-declension endings on the stem longiōr-

check.ask: Give the accusative singular and the nominative plural of *longior*.

teach.title: -ior or -ius? the noun decides
teach.say: This is where beginners slip. The choice between *-ior* and *-ius* has nothing to do with the meaning: it follows the gender of the noun the adjective describes. *Gladius* is masculine and *hasta* feminine, so both take *-ior*: *gladius longior*, *hasta longior*. *Scūtum* is neuter, so it takes *-ius*: *scūtum brevius*. Find the noun first, then choose the ending.

check.ask: *scūtum* is neuter. Which ending does its comparative take, *-ior* or *-ius*, and why?

teach.title: Using it: quam = than
teach.say: To name the other side of the comparison, use *quam*: *fluvius longior est quam via*. Whatever case the first side is in, the second side takes the same one — *Iūlius Mēdum altiōrem quam Dāvum esse putat* has both names in the object form.

check.ask: Dominī laetiōrēs sunt quam ___. The side after *quam* takes the same case as the side before it. (servus, more than one)

more.text: The comparative's ablative singular is *-e* (*longiōre*), its genitive plural *-um*, its neuter plural *-a* (*longiōra*): it follows the consonant-stem pattern, not the *-ī, -ium, -ia* of ordinary 3rd-declension adjectives.

Instead of *quam*, Latin can put the second thing in the ablative of comparison (the 'than' form: illo fortior = braver than he) with no *quam* at all: *gladius pīlō longior est* — its own skill. On its own the comparative can mean *rather* or *too*: *via longior* — a rather long road. Adjectives in *-eus / -ius* (*idōneus* suitable) use *magis* (more) instead: *magis idōneus*.

The learner's notes (week 12): the masculine and feminine nominative singular add *-ior* to the stem whatever the adjective's type (*īnfirmior, pigrior, gravior, sapientior*), the neuter adds *-ius* (*plēnius, gravius, pulchrius*); every other form adds a 3rd-declension ending after *-ior-*; the point of comparison follows *quam* (*vir īnfirmior est quam fēmina*). Ørberg (chapters XII–XIII): *altior, longior, brevius* are comparatives; *longior quam cēterae viae* — longer than the other roads.
